list.listitem: Neurofibromatosis 1 (NF1) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by multiple cafe-au-lait spots, inguinal and axillary freckling, neurofibromas (tumors of peripheral nerves), and Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas). C
An annual ophthalmology examination is recommended. C
Screen for learning disabilities in children with NF1. C
Treatment is primarily based on controlling or relieving symptoms. C
Immunotherapy holds promise for treating plexiform neurofibromas. B
The relative risk for other cancers is increased. B

background.definition: Neurofibromatosis is a group of 3 genetically-distinct disorders that cause tumors to grow in the nervous system. NF1, previously known as von Recklinghausen disease, is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by multiple cafe-au-lait spots, inguinal and axillary freckling, neurofibromas (tumors of peripheral nerves), and Lisch nodules (pigmented hamartomas of the iris). NF1 accounts for 96% of cases of neurofibromatosis. This chapter will not discuss neurofibromatosis 2 (NF2) or schwannomatosis; these disorders account for about 3% and <1% of cases, respectively. There is a recent clinical guideline on this condition.

list.listitem: Birth incidence: 1 in 2699 (range 1 in 960 to 1 in 5681)
A similar pooled NF1 birth incidence of 1 in 2662 (95%CI 1 in 1968 to 1 in 3601) was found in a meta-analysis of 12 studies.
1 in 3500 to 4500 population prevalence

Authors of the above meta-analysis found a pooled NF1 prevalence of 1 in 3164 (95%CI 1 in 2132 to 1 in 4712). Prevalence was higher in screening vs. medical record-based studies (1 in 2020 and 1 in 4329, respectively).

Plexiform neurofibromas (PNs) are often larger, more diffuse growths that arise from multiple nerves and sometimes involve connective tissue and skin folds. Authors of a systematic review identified 5 large registry/surveillance studies, each involving >19,000 individuals, and found a prevalence of associated PNs in patients with NF1 of 0-29.6%. PNs carried increased mortality risk and were associated with high use of analgesics. The post-surgical complication rate was approximately 17-19% and recurrence rate following surgery was 18-68%.

Individuals with NF1 are at higher risk of many types of tumors including malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (a type of soft-tissue sarcoma), optic and non-optic gliomas and many other cancers, discussed in the section on prognosis, natural history.

The American College of Medical Genetics (ACMG) and Genomics Professional Practice and Guidelines committee reported an association for individuals with NF1 of malignant gliomas, gastrointestinal stromal tumors. (GIST), rhabdomyosarcoma, thyroid, and malignant fibrous histiocytoma based on epidemiologic evidence and pheochromocytoma, somatostatinomas, and juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia based on genetic evidence.

NF1-associated vasculopathy occurs in 0.4% to 6.4% of patients with estimates of cerebrovascular vasculopathy of 2% to 5%. Types of vasculopathy reported include renal artery stenosis, aneurisms, arteriovenous malformation, and cardiac valve abnormalities.
Osteoporosis is more common in patients with NF1 and occurs at an earlier age than the general population.
Headache, epilepsy, and sleep disturbance/disorder are more common in adults with NF1, based on insurance-claim data.

Authors of a systematic review reported an overall lifetime prevalence of epilepsy of 5.4% in patients with NF1 (3.7% in children with NF1), with focal with or without bilateral tonic-clonic seizures being the most common seizure type. Structural causes were identified in half of cases (114/226) and causes included low-grade gliomas, mesial temporal sclerosis, malformation of cortical development, dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor, and cerebrovascular lesions.

Quality-of-life score for family and 910 patients with NF were lower compared to 6404 healthy controls based on a meta-analysis of 12 studies. NF had negative effects on physical function, bodily pain, mental health, social function and general health.
Autosomal dominant with wide phenotypic variability; half of children of a parent with neurofibromatosis will have the condition.
Pathogenic variants in the NF1 gene appear to correlate with the phenotype and genotype.

Due to the large size of the NF1 gene, a variety of mutations have been reported and several genotype-phenotype correlations have been identified. About 85% to 90% of cases are due to point mutations, 5% to 10% are microdeletions, and 2% are exon deletions or duplications. Microdeletions are associated with an increased number of dermal fibromas, more severe learning disabilities, and higher risk of cardiovascular and malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors.
Fifty percent of cases arise from de novo mutations.
Mutations in NF1 gene on chromosome 17q11.2. This gene produces neurofibromin, a tumor repressor protein produced in nerve cells.

Neurofibromin functions as a negative regulator of RAS/MAPK and PI3K/mTOR signaling pathways. Loss of neurofibromin results in increased protooncogene ras which can lead to tumorigenesis. A detailed discussion of the molecular pathways can be found in the cited reference.

Neurofibromas arise from nonmyelinating-type Schwann cells but also incorporate additional cell types and structural elements making it difficult to understand their origin and developmental mechanisms.
NF1 is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by multiple cafe-au-lait spots, inguinal and axillary freckling, neurofibromas (tumors of peripheral nerves), and Lisch nodules. C
Genetic testing can be performed to confirm the diagnosis and assist in screening family members, but a negative test does not completely exclude the diagnosis as it may also represent mosaicism. C
Routine neuroimaging of the brain is not recommended. Obtain a head MRI if the patient has visual changes, persistent headaches, seizures, marked increasing hydrocephalus, or a PN on the head. C
Screen for learning disabilities in children with NF1. C
An annual ophthalmology examination is recommended. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Mucocutaneous melanocytic macules and intestinal hamartomatous polyps
Epidermal and connective tissue nevi, hamartomatous overgrowth, hyperostosis
Multiple schwannomas, but not involving vestibular nerve
Cafe-au-lait spots, autonomous endocrine hyperfunction (eg, precocious puberty), and polyostotic fibrous dysplasia
SPRED1 mutation; cafe-au-lait spots, axillary freckling, and macrocephaly; no Lisch nodules or neurofibromas
Multiple lentigines, ECG conduction abnormalities, ocular hypertelorism, pulmonary stenosis, genitalia abnormalities, growth retardation, deafness, PTPN11 missense mutations
Mucous membrane neuromas, pheochromocytoma, medullary carcinoma of thyroid, GI ganglioneuromatosis
White forelock, cutaneous pigmentation and depigmentation with hyperpigmented borders of the unpigmented areas
Pigmented macules of glans penis, multiple lipomas and hemangiomas, macrocephaly
Multiple fibromas in skin, SC tissue, skeletal muscle, bones, viscera

list.listitem: The National Institutes of Health Consensus Development Conference on Neurofibromatosis (1987) set forth diagnostic criteria for NF1 which are met if two or more of the following are found: 1) Six or more café-au-lait macules over 5 mm in greatest diameter in prepubertal individuals and over 15 mm in greatest diameter in postpubertal individuals, 2) Two or more neurofibromas of any type or one PN, 3) Freckling in the axillary or inguinal region, 4) Optic glioma, and 5) Two or more Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas); a distinctive osseous lesion such as sphenoid dysplasia or thinning of long bone cortex with or without pseudarthrosis; or a first-degree relative (parent, sibling, or offspring) with NF-1 by the above criteria.

Diagnostic criteria were revised using a Delphi process that began with 76 international experts in 2018 and ended with final revision with 74/76 participants, and publication in 2021. The revised criteria specify that the diagnostic criteria for NF1 are met if two or more of the listed criteria are found for an individual with no parent with NF1, but for individuals who have a parent with NF1, having only one or more of the criteria is sufficient for diagnosis. In addition, the final criterion listed was divided into two and modified, and an additional criterion was added. The final recommended criteria for diagnosis are the first 4 listed above plus: 5) Two or more iris Lisch nodules identified by slit lamp or two or more choroidal abnormalities defined as bright, patchy nodules imaged by optical coherence tomography/near-infrared reflectance imaging, 6) A distinctive osseous lesion such as sphenoid dysplasia, anterolateral bowing of the tibia, or pseudarthrosis of a long bone, and 7) A heterozygous pathogenic NF1 variant with a variant allele fraction of 50% in apparently normal tissue such as white blood cells.

The consensus group also provided diagnostic criteria for mosaic NF1: 1) A pathogenic heterozygous NF1 variant with a variant allele fraction of significantly less than 50% in apparently normal tissue such as white blood cells AND one other NF1 diagnostic criterion, but no parent with NF1, 2) An identical pathogenic heterozygous NF1 variant in two anatomically independent affected tissues (in the absence of a pathogenic NF1 variant in unaffected tissue), 3) A clearly segmental distribution of café-au-lait macules or cutaneous neurofibromas and either another NF1 diagnostic criterion (except a parent fulfilling diagnostic criteria for NF1) or a child fulfilling diagnostic criteria for NF1, 4) Only one NF1 diagnostic criterion from the following: freckling in the axillary and inguinal region, optic pathway glioma, two or more Lisch nodules or two or more choroidal abnormalities, distinctive osseous lesion typical for NF1, two or more neurofibromas or one PN AND a child fulfilling the criteria for NF1 .
Suspect NF1 in a child with multiple cafe-au-lait spots; note that 1 to 2 cafe-au-lait patches occur in 10% of general population.
Ask about family history of neurofibromatosis.

Examine skin for cafe-au-lait spots (80% of patients with NF1 have more than 5 cafe-au-lait spots by 1 year of age), inguinal/axillary freckling (90%), and neurofibromas (>99% with neurofibromas, 25%-50% with PN).
Plexiform or complex neurofibromas are deeper benign lesions of the peripheral nerve sheath surrounding multiple nerve fascicles that create an irregular thickened subcutaneous mass that often feels like a bag of worms.

The National Institutes of Health Consensus Development Conference on Neurofibromatosis set forth diagnostic criteria for NF1 which are met if two or more of the following are found: six or more café-au-lait macules over 5 mm in greatest diameter in prepubertal individuals and over 15 mm in greatest diameter in postpubertal individuals; two or more neurofibromas of any type or one plexiform neurofibroma; freckling in the axillary or inguinal region; optic glioma; two or more Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas); a distinctive osseous lesion such as sphenoid dysplasia or thinning of long bone cortex with or without pseudarthrosis; or a first-degree relative (parent, sibling, or offspring) with NF-1 by the above criteria.
Neither the number nor size of the cafe-au-lait spots is associated with disease severity.

Authors of a case-control study with 110 cases and 110 controls found that those with 10 or more subcutaneous neurofibromas (19% of the case population) were more likely to have internal neurofibromas and axonal neuropathy with slowed conduction velocities. A score based on 4 clinical findings (at least two subcutaneous neurofibromas, age ≤30 years, absence of cutaneous neurofibromas, and fewer than six café-au-lait spots) was useful in predicting internal neurofibromas (area under the curve 0.75 in both development and validation samples).

Examine for skeletal changes: 10% to 26% of patients with NF1 have scoliosis, 2% have vertebral angulation or limb abnormalities. Other skeletal manifestations include pseudoarthritis, nonossifying fibromas, sphenoid dysplasia at birth, and decreased bone mineralization.

Neurologic manifestations include epilepsy, sensorineural hearing loss, cerebrovascular disease, increased intracranial pressure, spinal cord compression, autism, attention deficit disorder and intellectual impairment.

Cognitive impairment is a common complication of NF-1 and occurs in up to 60% of patients. Learning disabilities are reported in 30%-65% of children with NF-1. Authors of a meta-analysis of 11 studies found a significantly lower IQ in children with NF-1 compared to controls. In another meta-analysis, large deficits were observed in general intelligence and smaller deficits in the cognitive domain of emotion comparing patients with NF1 to typically-developing or unaffected siblings across different age groups.

Ophthalmologic manifestations include Lisch nodules and optic pathway glioma. Perform a visual screening and examination for poor visual acuity, strabismus, proptosis, and pale optic discs.
Orbitofacial neurofibromas can adversely affect vision.

Refer for an annual ophthalmology examination with slit-lamp until age 8 years, then every 2 years thereafter, to look for Lisch nodules (in >90% adults with NF1; appear as yellow to brown dome-shaped elevations on the surface of the iris that do not affect vision) and optic gliomas (15-20% of patients have optic gliomas, but only 5% are symptomatic from optic glioma).

Endocrine manifestations include precocious puberty, pheochromocytoma, and both short or tall stature (the latter related to growth hormone excess). Plot growth on neurofibromatosis growth charts. Patients with NF1 tend to have short stature (1/3) and macrocephaly.

Ninety five percent of NF1 cases can be diagnosed by clinical criteria by the patient's 11th birthday. However, consider genetics referral for possible molecular testing (which can detect 95% of NF1 mutations) if a definitive diagnosis is uncertain.

High-resolution ultrasound may be useful for screening patients with NF1 for PNs to identify the subgroup of patients who could benefit from regular follow-up. In one study, of 17 patients with asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic NF1, severe involvement of the peripheral nervous system with multiple PNs was observed in seven.

Routine neuroimaging of the brain is not routinely recommended. Obtain a head MRI if the patient has visual changes, persistent headaches, seizures, marked increasing hydrocephalus, or a PN on the head. [18F]-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) may be helpful in predicting malignant transformation in children with PNs.

Authors of a study of 21 patients with NF1 comparing fMRI and PDG-PET/CT imaging for characterizing 55 peripheral nerve sheath tumors as benign or malignant found specificities for fMRI of 94% using apparent diffusion coefficient minimum ≤1 and 83% for FDG-PET/CT using maximum standardized uptake values >3.2 while maintaining sensitivities at 100%; 19 (35%) of the tumors were malignant.

Pooled sensitivity for differentiation of malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors in patients with NF1 was higher with FDG-PET vs. MRI (0.99 vs. 0.85, respectively), but specificity was higher with MRI (0.53 vs. 0.85, respectively) based on one meta-analysis.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 43 studies found absence of a target sign on MRI had the highest sensitivity (0.99, 95% CI 0.94-1.00) for ruling out malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors while ill-defined margins (0.94, 95% CI 0.88-0.98) and perilesional edema (0.95, 95% CI 0.83-1.00) showed highest specificity. The authors suggested that biopsy could be omitted for tumors displaying the presence of a target sign and absence of ill-defined margins and perilesional edema.

For FDG-PET, these authors found that SUVmax and tumor-to-liver ratio showed similar accuracy with a sensitivity of 0.94, 95% CI 0.91-0.97 and 0.93, 95% CI 0.87-0.97, respectively; specificity was 0.81, 95% CI: 0.76-0.87 and 0.79, 95% CI: 0.70-0.86 respectively. SUVmax ≥3.5 yielded the best accuracy (sensitivity 0.99, 95% CI 0.93-1.00 and specificity 0.75, 95% CI 0.56-0.90).
Including T2-hyperintensities on brain MRI may increase accuracy of diagnosis, especially in young children.
MRI with volumetric analysis is recommended to evaluate tumor size in clinical trials, with a 20% volume change as an indication of an increase or decrease in tumor size.

Magnetic resonance angiography is recommended by the ACMG guidelines for evaluation of renovascular hypertension in patients with NF1 with spiral CT and CT angiography considered for patients with impaired renal function (GFR <30mL/min).
Neurofibromatosis is clinically diagnosed. Suspect NF1 in a child with multiple cafe-au-lait spots.

Half the children who have NF1 and no known family history of NF1, and almost all the children with a parent with NF1, meet diagnostic criteria by 1 year of age. Almost all cases of NF1 can be diagnosed by the time the patient is 8 years old.
Treatment is primarily based on controlling or relieving symptoms. Surgically resect painful, disfiguring, or malignant tumors. C
Treatment of PN and neurofibromatosis-associated tumors includes strategies that target specific genetic or molecular events involved in tumorigenesis associated with NF1. C

Treat symptomatic optic gliomas with chemotherapy. Children with NF1 with progressive low-grade glioma responded to carboplatin and vincristine better than non-NF1 children with progressive low-grade glioma, with better event free survival but not overall survival; NF1 patients also had decreased Grade 3 or 4 toxicities compared with non-NF1 patients.
It is unclear whether adjunctive chemotherapy or radiation therapy in addition to surgery benefit patients with malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors based on the limited evidence available.

Various molecular targeted agents are under investigation for treating PNs. These include selumetinib and mirdametinib (MEK inhibitors), binimetinib and trametinib (MEK1/2 inhibitor), and cabozantinib (VEGFR2 inhibitor). The primary outcomes are volumetric response, toxicity, and event-free survival; most trials are in phase 2. Cutaneous reactions to MEK inhibitors are common; in children, these include dermatitis, acneiform eruptions, and paronychia.

Selumetinib, an oral selective inhibitor of RAS-mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) 1 and 2, may reduce tumor volume and disease progression in children with NF1-related PNs that are characterized by elevated MAPK signaling.

In a systematic review and meta-analysis of 5 trials with 126 children with NF1, the pooled objective response rate to selumetinib was 73.8% (95% CI 57.3%-85.5%) and the disease control rate was 92.5% (95% CI 66.5%-98.7%), although trial evidence was rated as low to moderate quality. The most common adverse events were diarrhea (pooled rate 63.8%, 95% CI 52.9%-73.4%) and an increase in creatine kinase levels (pooled rate 63.3%, 95% CI 35.6%-84.3%).

Authors of a systematic review of 92 registered clinical trials involving 4636 subjects also found selumetinib to be the most effective medication for treating inoperable or progressive PNs with a partial response reported in approximately 68%-71% of individuals age 2 years and older.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 10 trials with 268 patients with NF1 and inoperable PN found a disease control rate of 96.8% (95% CI 90.8-99.7%) with only 1.4% (95% CI 0-4.3%) showing progressive disease with selumetinib. The pooled pain improvement rate was 75.3% (95% CI 56.2-90.9%) and 77.8% (95% CI 63.1-92.5%) had motor improvement. Adverse events included diarrhea in 62.5% and vomiting in 54.5%.

In long-term follow-up of 74 children treated with selumetinib (median duration 57.5 28-day cycles), responses were sustained in 59% lasting ≥ 12 cycles and durable improvement was seen in tumor pain intensity and pain interference. No previously unreported adverse events occurred, although some patients developed an adverse event after several years of treatment.

In a phase 2 trial of mirdametinib including 19 patients 16 years and older with NF1 and progressive or symptomatic PNs, 8 of 19 (42%) achieved a partial response of the target PN by course 12 (4-week courses) that included reduced pain, and 10 (53%) had stable disease.

Similarly, in a phase 2 trial of cabozantinib in patients 16 years and older with progressive or inoperable, symptomatic PNs, 8 of 19 (42%) had a partial response (defined as a 20% or more reduction in target lesion volume on MRI after 12 cycles of therapy). Common adverse events included gastrointestinal toxicity, hypothyroidism, fatigue and palmar plantar erythrodysesthesia.
Surgical resection is recommended for painful or disfiguring tumors (neurofibromas, schwannomas) or tumors that may become cancerous.
Surgery is the treatment for high-grade malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors. In one case series, gross total resection of malignant peripheral nerve sheath sarcomas improved survival.

Spinal surgery with fusion can be successfully performed for patients with NF1 and dystrophic scoliosis, however data are sparse. Authors of a systematic review identified 30 studies describing 761 patients with at least 2-year follow-up and found a non-neurological complication rate of 14.0%, primarily dural tears and wound infections, an immediate postoperative neurological deficit rate of 2.1%, and permanent neurological deficit rate of 1.2%. Over time, loss of correction commonly occurred and 21.5% required revision surgery, most commonly for implant-related complications. Of the 5 papers reporting validated patient-reported outcome measures, there was improvement in mental health, self-image, and activity domains.
There is no evidence supporting the use of laser therapy to remove cafe-au-lait spots.
Laser therapy can be used to remove neurofibromas but reports on success are largely limited to case series. Carbon dioxide laser ablation can result in depigmentation and scarring.

In a case series with 19 patients with removal of 309 2-4 mm cutaneous NFs using 4 different modalities - radiofrequency needle coagulation, 755 nm alexandrite laser with suction, 980 nm diode laser, and intratumoral injection of 10 mg/mL deoxycholate – authors found each modality significantly reduced or cleared the NFs although there was large variation between tumors and participants. Alexandrite laser and deoxycholate were fast and least painful and the 980 nm laser was most painful. At 3-6 months, there was no evidence of growth stimulation from the treatments and no scarring or adverse events > grade 2

Authors of a meta-analysis of 6 RCTs demonstrated that mind-body therapies were associated with improved physical, psychological, and environmental quality of life (QOL) in patients with NF which was maintained at 6-months follow-up.

In a single-blind RCT with 31 patients with NF randomized to an 8-week group mind-body video intervention, home practice of relaxation skills occurred on an average of 28.55 days (SD = 10.79) and appreciation skills on an average of 24.39 days (SD = 13.48) over the 49-day treatment period; there was significant association between frequency of relaxation response-eliciting skills practice and physical QOL at the 6-month follow-up.

Similarly, a virtual mind-body program delivered to 25 adolescents with NF compared to an education-only control group resulted in high satisfaction in both groups but the group randomized to the mind-body intervention showed greater baseline to post-treatment improvements in QOL in the domains of physical health, psychological health, social relations and environmental, improvements maintained through 6-month follow-up.

In an RCT of 228 patients with NF treated with eight 90-minute virtual group sessions of either a Relaxation Response Resiliency Program (3RP) or a health education program, patients in both groups improved in QOL scores; however, at 12 months, greater improvement occurred in the 3RP group for physical health, social relationships and environmental QOL scores. 3RP also appears to lower rates of clinically significant depressive symptoms based on a second study.

In a 12-week phase 2 trial of 6 children with NF1 who were experiencing muscle weakness and fatigue, L-carnitine supplementation (1000 mg daily oral levocarnitine tartrate) was associated with improved strength in most and a mean 10% increase in long jump distance and 6-minute walking distance (95% CI 5.9-75.4); there were no reported adverse events.

If a child shows evidence of a learning disability (seen in 30%-60%), his or her school should evaluate for IQ, verbal, and spatial skills and provide appropriate services through Individual Education Plans.

Refer patients with NF1 to a clinician skilled in the management of NF1. Consider referring children with 3 or more cafe-au-lait spots and no other signs or symptoms of NF1 to a neurofibromatosis clinic as they may have mosaic NF1 or NF2.
Refer for an annual ophthalmology examination with slit-lamp until the age of 8 years, then every 2 years thereafter.
Retinal artery aneurysms have been reported in patients with NF1 and hypertension; endovascular treatment was successful in one case report.

Authors of a systematic review identified 564 patients with optic gliomas (low-grade astrocytomas of the optic pathway) and found that among the 69 patients undergoing observation, 87% demonstrated stable acuity. In the chemotherapy studies, 27.3% (72/264) demonstrated improved acuity/visual field and/or visual-evoked potential amplitudes, 39.4% (104/264) stable acuity, and 33.3% (88/264) deterioration. In radiation and surgical treatment studies, worsening visual acuity was reported at 90.9% (10/11) and 73.3% (11/15), respectively.

In a retrospective study of 25 eyes of children with NF1-associated optic gliomas, use of everolimus resulted in the majority exhibiting stabilization with 4 eyes improved and 2 showing worsening visual acuity.

Brainstem mass lesions can occur and were reported in one case series in 23 (18.4%) of 125 children with NF1 who underwent brain imaging. Of the 23 children, only 8 underwent tumor-specific treatment and, at a median follow-up period of 67 months for the 17 untreated patients and 102 months for the 6 patients who received therapy, only one previously untreated patient experienced progression and all but one remained alive

Pheochromocytoma and/or paraganglioma are associated with NF1. In one case series of tumor resection in 71 patients, including 26 patients with NF1, patients with NF1 had more volatile intraoperative hemodynamic courses with more severe postoperative complications.
NF1 is a progressive disorder, but with wide clinical variation. C

Children with NF1 appear to have impairments in intelligence, academic skills, visuospatial skills, social competence, and attention; it is not clear if there are impairments in memory, motor functioning, language, or executive functions. B
Individuals with NF1 have a greater likelihood of hospitalization and development of malignancies compared to the general population. A
NF1 is associated with an 8- to15-year reduction in average life expectancy in both men and women, primarily due to malignant neoplasms and cardiovascular causes. A

Based on two population studies, the incident number of cafe-au-lait spots increased until age 30 to 40 years, and then decreased in number. The incident number of cutaneous neurofibromas increased with age, while the number of subcutaneous neurofibromas remained steady after 40 years of age.

Among patients with PNs, authors of a systematic review found a broad range of complications for these lesions including pain (35-53%), disfigurement/physical deformity (30-73%), and neurologic deficit/loss of function (13-46%). Most lesions grew (20% volume increase; 69%-86%). In one of the reviewed studies, potentially life-threatening complication included airway compression (4/59 or 7%) and spinal cord compression (14/59 or 24%). In another, patients with NF1 and symptomatic PN had a higher mortality rate that those with NF1 without PN (5/154 or 3.2% vs. 2/366 or 0.5%).

In a population-based study in Denmark, children with NF1 were less likely than NF-1 free persons to attain higher education (> 12 years) and were significantly delayed in graduating mandatory school education.

Individuals with NF1 also have a greater likelihood of hospitalization (RR 2.3, 95% CI 2.2-2.5) compared with general population controls based on a population-based study from Denmark. 32107470 There was an absolute excess risk for all 12 main diagnostic groups, including disorders of the nervous system (14.5% of all excess risk), benign (13.6%) and malignant neoplasms (13.4%), and disorders of the digestive (10.5%) and respiratory systems (10.3%).
There is no tendency for cafe-au-lait spots to become malignant.

The lifetime risk of developing malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors is 8% to 13%, particularly from PNs, and predominately in 20- to 35-year-olds. Authors of a meta-analysis of 59 retrospective studies involving 3602 patients with malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors found that those with NF1 compared to sporadic cases had substantially higher risk of all-cause mortality (HR 1.6, 95% CI 1.4 to 1.8) and disease-specific mortality (HR 1.5, 95% CI 1.2 to 1.9). Those with low-grade peripheral nerve sheath tumors have a 10-year survival rate of 100% while those with high-grade tumors have a 5-year survival rate of 20%.

The relative risk (RR) of other malignancies appears increased for cancer of the esophagus (3.3), stomach (2.8), colon (2.0), liver (3.8), lung (3.0), bone (19.6), thyroid (4.9), malignant melanoma (3.6), non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (3.3), chronic myeloid leukemia (6.7), female breast (2.3) and ovary (3.7).

The predominant histology for breast cancer associated with NF1 is invasive ductal carcinoma but women with NF1 have a poorer 5-year survival. Women with NF1 who are under age 50 years have a five-fold increased risk of breast cancer and present with more advanced disease.
Individuals with NF1 are at higher risk of central nervous system neoplasms, the most common of which are low-grade optic pathway gliomas (15% of children with NF1).

In a retrospective case series of 64 children with NF1 who had 100 probable brain non-optic pathway tumors, 25% were symptomatic at diagnosis and most (63%) progressed with average time from diagnosis to stabilization or decrease in tumor size of 2.34 years. Most tumors were located in the basal ganglia region, cerebellum, medulla and midbrain areas and of the 19 that were assessed with histopathology, all were confirmed as neoplasms.

In a retrospective, cross sectional study of 133 children with NF1 and brainstem gliomas from 4 referral centers, average age at diagnosis was 7.2 years and most (54%) were asymptomatic.Thirty-one of the 61 symptomatic children received treatment for their tumor and only 9 of the children who were initially asymptomatic were treated because of progressive tumor enlargement. Overall survival was 85% for the tumor-directed therapy group and no deaths were reported in the untreated or CSF diversion groups.

However, authors of a follow-up study of 5+ year survivors of childhood glioma found that late mortality among the 147 glioma survivors with NF1 was twice that of the 2629 other survivors at 46.3% (95% CI 23.9-62.2%) vs. 18.0% (95% CI 16.1-20.0%), respectively, largely due to subsequent malignancies. Survivors with NF1 were also more likely to report psychosocial impairments, neurocognitive deficits, and socioeconomic difficulties compared with survivors without NF1.

Individuals with NF1 have an increased overall hazard ratio (HR) of 2.6 (95% CI 1.9-3.6) for intestinal tumors compared to general population, especially for tumors of the small intestine (HR 15.6; 95% CI 6.9-35.1).

Refer for an annual ophthalmology examination with slit-lamp until age 8 years, then every 2 years thereafter to look for Lisch nodules (in >90% adults with NF1) and optic gliomas (15% of patients have optic gliomas, but only 5% are symptomatic from optic glioma).
Plot growth on neurofibromatosis growth charts. Patients with NF1 tend to have short stature (1/3) and macrocephaly.

After the diagnosis is made, follow-up with annual blood pressure (hypertension may be associated with renal artery stenosis in 2%, pheochromocytoma in 2%, or aortic stenosis), a check of head circumference in infants/children (macrocephaly is usually benign, though can rarely be caused by aqueductal stenosis in 1.5% of patients), an examination for signs of precocious puberty (which may be associated with optic glioma or hypothalamic lesion), and a neurodevelopmental examination (50% of patients have learning disabilities).

The National Comprehensive Cancer Network guidelines recommend an annual mammogram starting at age 30 years with consideration of contrast-enhanced breast MRI between ages 30 and 50 years for women with NF1.

Pain, rapid growth, neurologic symptoms, and awareness of risk factors (deep, truncal location of a plexiform neurofibroma, germline microdeletion of the NF1 locus, or previous radiation) remain key for early detection of malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors. Fingertip or toe pain may indicate presence of glomus tumors and gastrointestinal complaints may signal GI tumors such as GIST.
MRI and PET scans can be used to monitor progression of PNs and watch for malignant transformation, optimal frequency is undetermined.
Consider prenatal genetic counseling and molecular testing if one parent has NF1 and the couple would like a prenatal diagnosis.
